hook.text: A summary and a plot describe the data you already have. To reason about data you haven't seen, you need probability... starting with what a probability even means.

half.text: Say a coin lands heads with probability one half. But a single flip is heads or tails. There's no half a head.

longrun.text: So read it the frequentist way, as the long run. A probability is the fraction of times something happens, when you repeat it over and over.

flips.text: That's easy to repeat in code. Flip a coin a hundred thousand times, and fifty thousand, one hundred and twenty-one come up heads.

share.text: Point five zero one. Close to a half... even though the first seven flips were all heads.

lln-in.text: So how long does the long run take?

lln.text: Here's the share of heads so far, after every one of five thousand flips.

early.text: After four flips, it's at three quarters. Out to a hundred, it still swings from forty percent to fifty-six.

late.text: After a thousand, it never strays more than a point and a half from one half.

law.text: That's the law of large numbers. The short run is noisy... the long run is stable.

memory.text: But it doesn't work by balancing out. After five heads in a row, a fair coin is still fifty-fifty. It has no memory.

swamp.text: A streak is never paid back. It just gets swamped by everything that comes after it.

table-in.text: Most probabilities change, though, the moment you learn something.

table.text: Here are a thousand users, split by plan, and by whether they churned this quarter.

overall.text: Across everyone, a hundred and fifty churned. Fifteen percent.

paid.text: Now condition on the plan. Of the five hundred paid users, thirty churned... six percent.

free.text: Of the five hundred free users, a hundred and twenty. Twenty-four percent.

zoom.text: That's all conditioning is. Keep only the rows where the condition holds, and take the fraction inside them.

split-in.text: And comparing those fractions tells you whether the two things are linked.

split.text: Draw each plan as a bar, split where its users churned.

flat.text: If knowing the plan told you nothing, both would split at the same height. Fifteen percent.

indep.text: That's independence: the chance given the plan is the same as the chance without it.

step.text: Here, the split jumps from six percent to twenty-four. Plan and churn are dependent, and that gap is information you can act on.

multiply.text: Independence is also what lets you multiply. Ten heads in a row is ten halves multiplied together... about one in a thousand.

test-in.text: And which way round you read a conditional matters more than it looks.

test.text: A disease affects one person in a thousand. A test for it is ninety-nine percent accurate, both ways. You test positive.

gut.text: What are the chances you have it? Your gut says ninety-nine percent. The answer is about nine.

walk.text: Walk a hundred thousand people through it. A hundred have the disease. Ninety-nine thousand, nine hundred don't.

caught.text: The test catches ninety-nine of the hundred.

flagged.text: But it also flags one percent of the healthy by mistake. That's nine hundred and ninety-nine false alarms.

lineup.text: Now line up everyone who tested positive. One thousand and ninety-eight people... and only ninety-nine of them are sick.

sim.text: Simulate two million people instead, and you get nine point one.

inverse.text: The gut answer reads the conditional backwards. Ninety-nine percent of sick people test positive. That does NOT mean ninety-nine percent of positives are sick.

bayes.text: Bayes' rule turns one into the other, and it can't work without the base rate: how common the disease was before anyone was tested.

neglect.text: Healthy people outnumber the sick nearly a thousand to one, so their false alarms beat the real cases ten to one. Forgetting that is base-rate neglect.

retest.text: So test the positives again, with a second, independent test. Ninety-eight of the real cases stay positive... and only about ten of the false alarms.

ninety.text: Now nine positives in ten are real. Ninety-one percent.

rule.text: So before you trust a positive, ask how rare the thing is.

doors.text: A game show has three doors. Behind one is a car, and behind the other two, goats. You pick a door.

host.text: Then the host, who knows where the car is, opens another door... and shows you a goat. Do you switch?

column.text: In nineteen ninety, a magazine columnist said yes: switching wins two times in three. Thousands of readers wrote in to tell her she was wrong.

cases.text: She was right. Your first pick hides the car one time in three.

goat.text: The other two times, you've picked a goat... so the host has to open the other goat. The door he leaves shut has the car.

knows.text: His choice isn't random. It depends on where the car is, and that's information.

games.text: Play a hundred thousand games in code. Staying wins thirty-three percent of them. Switching wins sixty-seven.

rv-in.text: So far, the outcomes have been labels. Heads, a goat, a positive. To average them, you need numbers.

rv.text: A random variable puts a number on each outcome. Flip two coins, and count the heads. Two, one, one... or zero.

die.text: Its most useful summary is the expected value, the long-run average. Take a loaded die that lands on six half the time, and on each other face a tenth.

weight.text: Multiply each face by its chance, and add. Four point five.

balance.text: Picture the chances as weights on a beam. It balances at four and a half... which isn't a face on the die, and isn't the likeliest roll, either. That's six.

rolls.text: Roll it half a million times in code, and the average comes out four point five.

spread.text: Its spread is the variance, the average squared distance from that mean. Three point two five. Its square root, the standard deviation, is about one point eight.

decide-in.text: And that long-run average is how you weigh a decision.

warranty.text: A store sells an eighty-dollar warranty. It pays out three hundred if the device fails, and fifteen percent of them do.

expect.text: So the expected payout is fifteen percent of three hundred, forty-five dollars. The store expects to keep thirty-five per warranty.

million.text: Sell a million in code, and the average profit is thirty-five dollars and five cents. Good for the store... and, on average, a losing bet for the buyer.

once.text: But an average is for a gamble you face many times. For one loss you couldn't survive, the spread matters MORE... which is why people buy insurance at all.

next.text: An expected value and a variance sum up one random variable. And many random variables share a handful of familiar shapes... the named distributions.
